newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian police say they avoided Venice "bloodbath".
newsitem.headline: Italian police say they avoided Venice "bloodbath".

text.p: Police commandos stormed the belltower in St Mark's Square in Venice on Friday and arrested eight armed Italian separatists who had occupied it in a bizarre independence bid.

"There is a sense of satisfaction because a bloodbath was avoided and because we think we thwarted possible future actions like this," Colonel Emilio Borghini, the paramilitary Carabinieri police commander in the canal city, told reporters.
"No shots were fired...We did not use tear gas or explosives," he said. "They didn't put up any resistance."

A crack team of 24 masked Carabinieri special forces, flown in from the western port of Livorno, ended the protest some five hours after the group of young men, many dressed in combat fatigues, broke into one of Venice's best-known landmarks.

Police said the group had commandeered a "vaporetto" ferry shortly after midnight to take them, a six-wheeled home-made armoured vehicle and a camper van down the Grand Canal to St Mark's Square, a magnet for millions of tourists.
Borghini said police had found one sub-machine gun and a quantity of ammunition and were investigating whether a weapon protruding from the armoured vehicle was real or fake.

The commander of the special forces unit, his face masked to shield his identity, told reporters food, wine, water and sleeping bags had also been found, suggesting the separatists had expected to hole up in the tower for a long siege.

The forces scaled part of the outside of the 99 metre (325 ft) tower by telescopic ladder. They entered through a low level balcony and used an internal staircase to the top, completing their entire blitz in just eight minutes.
Six of the protesters were arrested in the tower and two seized in the black and green armoured vehicle in the square.
One shouted "Long Live St Mark" in a Venetian accent as police led him off to cries from onlookers of "Shame" and "You should be thrown in the lagoon".
The eight face charges including membership of an armed band, subversion, kidnapping and illegal possession of weapons.
The Northern League, Italy's main separatist group which declared a symbolic separate state of "Padania" at a rally in Venice in September last year, described the protest as madness.
"Finding an armoured car and going to St Mark's Square to stand there and raise a little flag is no way to stage a revolution," League leader Umberto Bossi told Italian radio.
Other politicians, however, argued that the protest showed deeper malaise at the lack of movement towards federal reform.
"These are confusing times in the north, confusing enough to spark provocations in minds that are not very mature," Venice mayor Massimo Cacciari, a leftist, told Reuters.
"This has nothing to do with the League but with a general climate of confusion which leads some crazy people to do something as insane and dangerous as this," he said.
The group had raised a banner on the tower bearing the symbol of the lion of St Mark and issued a statement describing themselves as soldiers of the "Most Serene Republic of Venice".

"After 200 years, a regular unit of the Most Serene Venetian Army has tonight liberated St Mark's Square," the statement said. "The Most Serene Republic of Venice has been reborn today...Long live St Mark."
Police linked Friday's protest to a shadowy group that has interrupted state television news bulletins in the northeast Veneto region for two months with calls for a separate state.
The pirate broadcasts have spoken of a "spectacular action" in the canal city to mark next Monday's 200th anniversary of the fall of the Venice Republic.

Venice was for centuries a powerful independent power with territories stretching down the Adriatic and into the Middle East. Known as the "Most Serene Republic", it fell on May 12, 1797, when French forces of Napoleon Bonaparte entered the city.
